subject: operating-systems
title: Kernel responsibilities
summary: The kernel is the privileged core of an operating system that mediates hardware access and manages shared resources.

resources.title: Kernel (operating system)
resources.why: Covers kernel responsibilities, protection, resource management, and hardware access.

questions.prompt: Two runnable processes need CPU time. Which OS component decides when each runs?
options: CPU scheduler in the kernel
File-system directory parser
C compiler
Text editor
questions.answerKey: The CPU scheduler selects among runnable processes or threads according to the scheduling policy.
questions.explanation: Scheduling is a kernel responsibility; compilation, directory parsing, and editing do not choose CPU execution order.

questions.prompt: Why does an OS mediate access to a disk controller instead of allowing every application to program it directly?
options: To make every disk request execute in constant time
To enforce permissions and coordinate shared device access
Because disk controllers only work during boot
Because applications cannot perform file operations
questions.answerKey: Kernel mediation protects the device and lets the OS coordinate requests and enforce access rules.
questions.explanation: Applications can request file I/O; direct hardware access is not required and would weaken isolation.

questions.prompt: A process requests a new virtual-memory mapping. Which subsystem checks and manages the process's address-space mapping?
options: Source-code formatter
Shell command history
Kernel memory-management subsystem
Network name resolver
questions.answerKey: The kernel manages process address spaces and enforces mapping permissions; details vary by OS and allocator.
questions.explanation: Address-space mappings are memory-management work, not shell, formatting, or DNS work.

questions.prompt: A buggy user application writes to an invalid address and terminates, while unrelated processes continue. What most directly helps contain this fault?
options: Giving every process unrestricted physical-memory access
Running all applications with kernel privileges
Disabling page-fault handling
Protected address spaces and hardware-enforced access checks
questions.answerKey: Memory protection prevents an ordinary process from freely overwriting unrelated address spaces; a fault can be isolated to that process.
questions.explanation: Unrestricted access or kernel-mode applications would make failures more likely to affect the whole system.

questions.prompt: A proposed OS lets every process overwrite arbitrary physical memory to avoid copying overhead. What is the strongest objection?
options: It guarantees lower latency for all workloads
It prevents the CPU from executing arithmetic
It makes access permissions unnecessary but preserves security
It breaks isolation and can corrupt the kernel or other processes
questions.answerKey: Unrestricted physical-memory writes defeat protection and allow accidental or malicious corruption; any performance claim needs evidence and does not remove this risk.
questions.explanation: The central trade-off is not simply speed: memory isolation is a core reliability and security property.

questions.prompt: Name three kernel responsibilities. Then explain one concrete way the kernel helps isolate two processes.
questions.answerKey: Valid responsibilities include CPU scheduling, memory management, device/I/O management, and process management. Isolation can be enforced through separate virtual address spaces and access permissions, so one process cannot ordinarily read or overwrite another process's private memory.
questions.explanation: Credit specific responsibilities and a real isolation mechanism, not a vague statement that the kernel 'runs the computer'.
